question_text:
A 30-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of back pain beginning 2 hours ago. Beginning yesterday, he noticed that his eyes started appearing yellowish and his urine was darker than normal. Two months ago, he returned from a trip to Greece, where he lived before immigrating to the US 10 years ago. Three days ago, he was diagnosed with latent tuberculosis and started on isoniazid. He has worked as a plumber the last 5 years. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. Examination shows back tenderness and scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show:
Hematocrit 29%
Leukocyte count 8000/mm3
Platelet count 280,000/mm3
Serum
Bilirubin
Total 4 mg/dL
Direct 0.7 mg/dL
Haptoglobin 15 mg/dL (N=41–165 mg/dL)
Lactate dehydrogenase 180 U/L
Urine
Blood 3+
Protein 1+
RBC 2–3/hpf
WBC 2–3/hpf
Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's anemia?"?

                    ### Options

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with symptoms indicative of hemolysis, including sudden onset of back pain, yellowish eyes (scleral icterus), dark urine, low haptoglobin, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase. The presence of blood and protein in the urine suggests hemoglobinuria, a common result of hemolysis. The recent initiation of isoniazid for latent tuberculosis is significant, as isoniazid can induce oxidative stress in red blood cells. This stress can lead to hemolysis if there is an absence of reduced glutathione, which is crucial for neutralizing oxidative damage. The evidence paths confirm the interaction between isoniazid and glutathione, and the role of glutathione in protecting erythrocytes from oxidative damage. Therefore, the most likely underlying cause of this patient's anemia is the absence of reduced glutathione leading to hemolysis induced by isoniazid treatment.
